item.title: Xi highlights green path to development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Xi highlights green path to development Ecosystem's recovery, computer hub's progress in Inner Mongolia city hailed A first-time visitor looking across the Huangqihai Lake in northern China might find it hard to imagine its dry, exposed lake bed just 20 years ago. When President Xi Jinping visited the lakeside on Friday in Ulaanqab, a city in the Inner Mongolia autonomous region, the water stretched across more than 85 square kilometers. Fish had been detected again in May last year — a sign that the lake's ability to purify itself and sustain aquatic life was gradually recovering. Looking through binoculars at birds on the mudflats, Xi said: "There are quite a few birds. The aquatic ecosystem here has recovered well." The Huangqihai Lake nature reserve was the first stop on a fact-finding trip that also took Xi to the Qahar High-Tech Industrial Development Zone, where the city is expanding its green computing power industry. During the visit, Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, stressed the need to coordinate high-quality development with high-level environmental protection. Fed by 11 rivers, Huangqihai is an inland lake that came close to drying up following decades of drought and other pressures. In recent years, local authorities have dredged waterways feeding the lake, reduced agricultural pollution, restored vegetation and strengthened protection of the reserve. Xi asked whether production activities were still taking place around the lake. Local officials told him that activity in the core area was controlled to reduce human disturbance. He called for giving priority to natural restoration, supplemented by human intervention, in repairing degraded wetland ecosystems. Ban Xiuping, Party secretary of Qahar Right Wing Front Banner, where the lake is located, said local residents have a deep attachment to Huangqihai. Its recovery has helped stabilize agricultural incomes and improve people's living environment, she said. "I think General Secretary Xi's commitment to ecological restoration and conservation is rooted in his deep concern for the people," she said. For Ban, the next milestone would be the return of more fish species. Crucian carp have already been detected, and she hopes common carp and grass carp will follow. Friday's visit was Xi's fourth fact-finding trip to Inner Mongolia since 2012, following trips in 2014, 2019 and 2023. He has repeatedly called for protecting the region's lakes and pursuing the integrated conservation and restoration of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts. In 2023, he inspected Ulansuhai Nur in Bayannuur and urged sustained efforts to protect it. At Huangqihai, Xi called for sustained efforts to control sand and address overgrazing. He described the region's ecological protection as a national strategy benefiting both Inner Mongolia and the country as a whole. Wu Guoqing, deputy director of Inner Mongolia's forestry and grassland bureau, said the department's work in recent years has included controlling desertification, addressing overgrazing and tackling the destruction of forests and grasslands. According to figures released by the regional forestry and grassland bureau in June, Inner Mongolia's forest coverage has reached 21.98 percent, up 1.19 percentage points from 2021, while grassland vegetation coverage stood at 46.48 percent, its highest level this century. As Ulaanqab works to restore the Huangqihai Lake, it is also developing its computing power industry. Just 240 kilometers from Beijing in a straight line, Ulaanqab offers abundant renewable energy, a climate that allows natural cooling for nearly 10 months a year, and direct fiber-optic links to the capital. At the development zone, Xi learned about Inner Mongolia's progress in building a hub for the "East Data, West Computing" project, a national initiative linking computing power demand in eastern China with resources in western regions. He was also briefed on the development of the city's green computing power industry. Urlug, deputy director of the zone's economic development and investment promotion bureau, said the city's computing power industry has grown in stages. Huawei's arrival in 2013 brought Ulaanqab its first data center. For roughly a decade, the industry focused on storage and general-purpose computing. From 2023 to around the turn of 2026, the city moved into a second phase focused on intelligent computing — the processing capacity used for artificial intelligence — with upgrades to chips, technology and supporting facilities, Urlug said. The third phase, in his description, is closer coordination between computing power and electricity supply. "We are drawing on Ulaanqab's abundant renewable energy resources to develop a green intelligent computing power industry," he said. During the trip, Xi commended the industry's progress and called for extending industrial chains, deepening the integration of the digital and real economies, and translating computing power strengths into development gains. He also examined models of power and cooling systems and asked detailed questions about electricity and water efficiency. Liu Junping, deputy director of the zone's administrative committee, said Xi's attention to water conservation left a strong impression. "In developing computing capacity, we need to plan ahead," Liu said. "Ulaanqab is a water-scarce place. While saving energy, we must also save water." Xi called for efficient, green and safe development, stressing coordination between computing power, electricity supply and water use. He urged those working in the sector to ensure the sound construction and operation of computing centers, actively promote the green computing power industry, and make greater contributions to building Digital China and developing new quality productive forces. His discussions with officials and industry representatives included a warning about the way new industries expand. "What worries me most is disorderly development — everyone rushing in at once and then dispersing all at once, which further dampens enthusiasm," Xi said. He also warned against blind competition and development that disregards local conditions. Urlug said: "Computing power is an emerging industry. We need to get involved early and plan ahead so it develops in an orderly way." The industry is also bringing talented people to Ulaanqab. Zan Deng, manager of the Inner Mongolia Huawang Data Center of Jiangsu Yangdian Science & Technology Co, moved to the city in 2024 to work on the project. More than 70 percent of the company's staff members there have been recruited from elsewhere, she said, with employees settling in the city. Zan was among the industry representatives whom Xi spoke with during the visit. Xi encouraged those present to pursue ambitious goals with patience and determination, describing them as a contingent advancing high-level scientific and technological self-reliance on a new "Long March". "As someone working in this industry, I feel deeply honored and proud to be part of this journey," Zan said. Contact the writers at mojingxi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: AI expands access to traditional medicine
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
AI expands access to traditional medicine Artificial intelligence is now being widely applied to enhance traditional medicine, making it more accessible, standardized and research-based, according to a report released on Sunday on the sidelines of the 2026 World Conference on Traditional Medicine in Beijing. Centuries-old traditional remedies have typically relied on wisdom passed down through a teacher-disciple tradition, and often lack the scientific rigor and diagnostic standards adopted by modern medicine. Li Haiyan, director of the Institute of Information on Traditional Chinese Medicine of the China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, which led the report, said that AI tools can turn accumulated practices into knowledge and data that can be stored, programmed and validated. She was speaking at the launch of the report examining AI's applications in the global development of traditional medicine. The report was initiated by the Global Alliance for Traditional and Integrative Medicine and was released during the 2026 World Conference on Traditional Medicine, which was held over the weekend. Premier Li Qiang also underlined the need to harness science and technology to accelerate the innovative development of traditional medicine. While addressing the opening ceremony of the conference on Saturday, he said China will promote the digital and intelligent transformation of TCM and encourage and support active participation of Chinese and foreign research institutions and enterprises. The report said that AI-empowered traditional medicine has entered a phase of rapid development, as a number of nations have incorporated the technology into broader health development strategies. In a sign of evolving technologies, a total of 3,030 AI-related traditional medicine patents have been published globally since 2000, and 6,882 high-quality academic papers have been released since 1990, the report said. China accounted for 80.4 percent of the patents and 47 percent of the academic papers, demonstrating the scale of the nation's research and technological advantage in this field, it added. In clinical practice, Li, the researcher, said that AI has been used to assist in examinations of a patient's tongue, pulse, facial appearance and other aspects, as well as in diagnosis. For some syndromes, AI-assisted tongue diagnosis has proved to be 85 to 92 percent accurate, with the ability to distinguish experience-based symptom descriptions such as "a reddish tongue". "Some digital twin models trained on the clinical experience, diagnostic reasoning and typical case records of renowned TCM practitioners have already been piloted in China's county-level TCM hospitals to expand access to quality TCM resources," she said. AI has also been used to digitalize the surveying, identification, cultivation and supply chain traceability of medicinal plants, accelerate the screening of active ingredients and analysis of drug mechanisms, and advance basic research in areas such as jing luo, also known as meridians, through which the body's energy is believed to circulate. Moreover, Li said AI has enabled more systematic reviews of ancient medical texts to bolster innovative inheritance of traditional practices. In one case cited in the report, researchers used deep learning-assisted in vivo imaging to observe dynamic changes in immune cells in mouse models after electroacupuncture stimulation, offering a new perspective on how acupuncture points regulate the immune system, said Chen Jianxin, a professor at Beijing University of Chinese Medicine. In addition to TCM, Chen said the report showcases AI-powered inheritance among traditional Korean medicine practitioners, as well as smart diagnostic devices for Ayurveda, the traditional system of medicine originating in India. Chen said the uneven development of digital capabilities globally has affected traditional medicine's adoption of AI. More efforts are needed to accumulate high-quality datasets, address language differences between countries as well as between ancient and modern times, provide clearer explanations of medical mechanisms, and promote the establishment of unified supervision regulations targeting AI-assisted traditional medicine, he added. wangxiaoyu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Canada looks to China as trade diversification gains momentum
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Canada looks to China as trade diversification gains momentum Ottawa building economy less vulnerable to pressure from Washington, experts say Canada is stepping up efforts to diversify its trade as a renewed tariff confrontation with the United States puts fresh pressure on Ottawa to broaden its economic relationships. The US imposed a 50 percent tariff on C$27.6 billion ($19.6 billion) worth of Canadian goods effective Aug 22, prompting Canada to impose matching counter-tariffs on selected US products from Sept 8. The Canadian government has since emphasized the need to diversify trade and reduce dependence on any single partner. On Sept 29, a US ban on nearly $1 billion in annual imports from Canada took effect, targeting most Canadian alcoholic beverages, some dairy products and certain motorcycles. US President Donald Trump recently described Canada as "very difficult to deal with" and said: "Canada would like to make a deal, but we're not satisfied with it." Ron Stagg, a professor of history at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies Canadian-American relations, said the Canadian response to the latest US tariffs was being driven not only by economic considerations but also by growing frustration with what Ottawa sees as continuing demands from Washington. "Up until now the Carney government has treated the American government as a tough negotiator that will respond to conciliatory steps," Stagg told China Daily. "However, it is clear now that every time Canada gives a little, the US makes new demands," he said. He said the trade confrontation would reinforce Canada's efforts to build an economy that was less vulnerable to US pressure. China has emerged as one of the most significant destinations in that effort, with bilateral trade showing stronger export momentum in the first half of this year and both governments moving to restore market access in several areas. Canadian exports to China rose 30.1 percent year-on-year to C$21.74 billion in the first half of 2026, while imports from China fell 5.8 percent to C$44.86 billion, according to a report released by the Canada China Business Council and the China Institute at the University of Alberta. Total merchandise trade reached C$66.6 billion, up 3.6 percent from a year earlier. Bijan Ahmadi, executive director and COO of the Canada China Business Council, told China Daily the "most significant takeaway from the first half of 2026 is that Canada-China trade became more export-oriented". But the change in imports does not necessarily point to a broad retreat from Chinese products, he said. "The import decline was not a uniform retreat from Chinese supply: consumer goods and electronics weakened, while machinery, batteries and vehicles continued to grow," Ahmadi said, adding that full-year data would be needed before drawing broader conclusions. The report described the relationship as expanding "selectively rather than uniformly".

item.title: Nation to revamp train numbering system
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
Nation to revamp train numbering system China will overhaul its train numbering system to accommodate the expansion of its railway network, changing the meaning of several familiar letter prefixes while keeping routes and schedules unchanged under the current timetable. The changes, to be introduced in late November and late December, will increase the number of available train numbers for bullet train services by nearly 40 percent, China State Railway Group, the national railway operator, said on Friday. For travelers, including international visitors, the key change is that letters long associated with one type of train will identify another. T and K, previously used for regular speed express and fast trains, will identify high-speed services with top operating speeds of 300 kilometers per hour and 200 to 250 km/h, respectively. G will identify Fuxing trains with a maximum operating speed of 350 km/h. The X prefix will be reserved for Fuxing trains operating above 350 km/h. However, no X series passenger services will begin operating in this round of changes, said Xu Yan, deputy director of the operator's passenger transport center. The overhaul follows substantial growth in railway services. Between 2014 and 2025, China's railway network expanded from 112,000 kilometers to 165,000 km, while the average number of passenger trains operating daily rose from 4,894 to 11,796. "During peak travel periods such as the May Day and National Day holidays, G series services use more than 90 percent of the available train numbers for that prefix," said Fan Mingxiang, deputy director of the operator's transport department. Wei Yuguang, a professor at Beijing Jiaotong University, said train numbers serve purposes far beyond helping passengers find their trains. "They are a common language for coordination across regions and departments," he said, explaining that each train's unique number is a basic unit for organizing transport, dispatching, passenger services and accounting. Even the length of a number matters. "Using three digits or four may mean just one extra word each time for a dispatcher, but repeated throughout the day, it adds considerably to the workload," Wei said. Pronunciation also needs to be considered. "If two train numbers sound very similar, that can cause problems in dispatching," he said. Wei said the new system builds on existing rules while making room for more trains and new services. It must accommodate both passenger and freight trains, including those operating across borders. Cross-border passenger services will also have their train numbers adjusted on domestic sections of their routes under the revised rules, the operator said. Regular speed passenger trains, tourist trains and some freight services will have their numbers changed in late November, followed by high-speed and other services in late December. The new train numbers will appear on 12306, China's official railway booking platform, when tickets go on sale, up to 15 days before departure. Onboard services, including quiet carriages and online meal ordering, will remain unchanged. For international visitors who rely on travel guides to plan their trips, older explanations of train prefixes may no longer apply after the changes. The operator urged passengers to check train numbers, departure and arrival stations, and schedules carefully.

item.title: Boost Sino-African educational ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
Boost Sino-African educational ties The future of China-Africa relations hinges significantly on the collaborative efforts of our universities. Universities are not merely institutions that hand out degrees; they are epicenters of knowledge, developers of human capital, incubators of innovation and custodians of cultural heritage. Higher education is being reshaped by artificial intelligence, automation, biotechnology, climate change, renewable energy and the fourth industrial revolution, all of which are redefining the skills that societies need. For Africa, these shifts present both opportunities and challenges. While the continent has the world's youngest population and enormous human potential, its universities still struggle due to limited access, quality issues, financial constraints, inadequate infrastructure and a widening gap between education and the labor market. The challenge is no longer about producing more graduates, but about cultivating graduates who can generate knowledge, create employment and devise solutions. China's remarkable transformation offers educational lessons. Decades of investment in education, science and technology have made Chinese universities global centers of innovation. Africa's task is not to duplicate that experience but to learn from it, adapt it and forge partnerships that leverage the unique strengths of both regions. Historically, university cooperation has focused on exchanges, scholarships, conferences and memoranda of understanding. While these remain useful, the focus should now move from exchange to transformation, from mobility to joint knowledge creation, from joint research outputs to patents and commercialization, and from agreements on paper to practical partnerships. We must explore what Chinese and African universities can achieve together that neither could do alone. We need partnerships that foster joint research programs, innovation hubs, laboratories, graduate schools and centers of excellence. This includes more joint PhDs and co-supervision, and deeper collaboration in AI, digital education, renewable energy, climate change, agriculture, health, manufacturing, engineering, entrepreneurship and the creative industries. The focus should be on African development priorities while addressing global challenges. Tanzania illustrates these possibilities. Our relationship with China dates back to the early 1960s, marked by infrastructure projects such as the Tanzania-Zambia Railway and now spanning scholarships, research collaboration and institutional partnerships. At the University of Dar es Salaam, cooperation through the Confucius Institute has promoted academic exchange, people-to-people and cultural understanding and capacity building. The lesson is clear: sustainable cooperation grows from mutual respect, shared interests and clearly defined practical outcomes. Future partnerships must evolve beyond traditional mobility and capacity-building toward co-creation and innovation — from student exchange to joint talent development, from academic visits to joint research, from technology transfer to joint innovation, from memoranda of understanding to measurable institutional outcomes, and from individual projects to strategic, long-term partnerships. Talent development is a critical area where China and Africa must intensify cooperation. Africa needs young people equipped to work with emerging technologies, launch enterprises and solve complex problems; China brings experience in large-scale human-capital development, technological education and innovation ecosystems. Our universities should build joint talent platforms linking students, academics, industry and government, with reciprocal mobility, joint master's and doctoral programs and blended-learning arrangements. The aim is a new generation of professionals who understand both societies. Digital transformation is another major frontier. China has deep experience in digital infrastructure, educational technology and large-scale online learning; African universities will benefit if cooperation addresses our realities: connectivity, affordability, devices, skills and the urban-rural divide. We should create joint China-Africa digital education platforms for cross-continental teaching and resource sharing. AI should also be a major area of collaboration. However, as we embrace AI, we must address ethics, academic integrity, data governance, privacy, equity and the responsible use of technology. Universities on both sides should develop technological capacity and ethical frameworks together. Partnerships must be judged by the knowledge and solutions they produce. China and Africa should define joint research agendas where interests converge: climate change and environmental sustainability; renewable energy and the energy transition; food security and agricultural transformation; public health; digital transformation and AI; critical minerals and value addition; manufacturing and industrialization; urbanization and sustainable cities; education and skills development; entrepreneurship and employment creation. The principle is simple: we should research jointly, and translate that into joint publications, patents, innovations, enterprises and policy solutions. China-Africa cooperation cannot be a one-way model of transfer. Our universities should embrace knowledge co-creation, with African and Chinese scholars as equal partners in defining questions, designing methods and translating findings into practice. The goal should not be "What can China do for Africa?" or "What can Africa do for China?", but "What can China and Africa do together for both and for humanity?" The next generation of cooperation should move beyond a collection of agreements toward a more integrated model that builds deeper strategic partnerships, brings researchers, students, industry and policymakers together through joint centers of excellence, and develops talent through scholarships, joint degrees, doctoral training, co-supervision and reciprocal mobility. The goal is to turn these networks and skills into joint innovation, translating research into products, enterprises, technologies and services. Ultimately, cooperation should be judged by what it produces — graduates, innovations, enterprises and practical solutions — rather than by the number of agreements signed or delegations exchanged. The frontiers of educational development are no longer bounded by individual institutions or national borders. They are defined by our capacity to connect knowledge, people and technology across them. Higher education must become a more strategic pillar of the China-Africa relationship. For Tanzania, we remain committed to strengthening cooperation with China not as a recipient of aid, but as a partner with whom we can co-create knowledge, develop talent and advance innovation. China-Africa university cooperation should move from partners in exchange to partners in development, from recipients of knowledge to co-creators of knowledge, and from isolated institutions into interconnected engines of transformation. As the Father of the Nation of Tanzania, Julius Nyerere, emphasized in his address, "the role of universities", more than six decades ago, universities in developing countries must not simply receive knowledge; they must contribute to it as well. His vision underscores the importance of mutual contribution and knowledge creation, a principle that remains central to China-Africa university cooperation today. Our greatest achievement will not be stronger universities but a generation of young Africans and Chinese equipped to build a more prosperous, innovative and shared future. The author is the vice-chancellor of the University of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The article is adapted from his keynote speech at the China-Africa University Presidents Forum on Frontiers of Education Development. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily. item.title: Cook says China is key to iPhone Duo's success
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Cook says China is key to iPhone Duo's success Apple's first foldable smartphone is manufactured exclusively in China and Chinese app developers are crucial to iPhone Duo's success, Tim Cook, Apple's executive chairman, said in a recent exclusive interview with China Daily in Beijing. The remarks underline the great importance of China to United States tech companies such as Apple, as China is not just a huge market, but also an innovation center and a key manufacturing hub for their global operations, experts said. Cook said Chinese developers' enthusiasm for the foldable device and China's manufacturing capabilities are part of the recipe behind iPhone Duo's success. "We are working with a number of developers and optimizing some of the things at (our) Shanghai developer center. The apps are extremely important to us, and we're helping hand in hand," he said, adding that Chinese developers play a critical role in that process and they're very innovative. "China's market for foldables is second to none," Cook added. As Apple's first foldable model, iPhone Duo is far more difficult to manufacture than previous products. According to Apple, the process requires strong manufacturing precision and design capabilities, and it manages that through close collaboration with suppliers. Bai Ming, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, said, "China's decades of experience in electronics manufacturing and its continued push to pursue advanced and smart manufacturing make it the only country capable of making complicated products such as iPhone Duo." Cook is on a multi-stop visit to China, touring cities including Guangzhou in Guangdong province, Beijing and Shanghai. On Friday, Cook said at a forum in Shanghai that China's artificial intelligence application landscape is showing unprecedented dynamism, and AI is already having a profound impact on Apple's supply chain. During the trip, the senior executive also said that Apple Intelligence — which incorporates Chinese tech company Alibaba's Qwen large language model — has received approval in China and a test version is set to launch later this month. On Thursday, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao met Cook in Beijing, where they exchanged views on issues including China-US economic and trade relations. Notably, Cook said that Apple will further expand its business in China. Cook's visit came amid a wave of top US business executives' recent visits to China. Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater Associates, also visited Beijing this week. Sean Stein, president of the US-China Business Council, said the planet's most innovative companies are concentrated in the US and China, which lays a solid foundation for wider cooperation. "Such collaboration stretches well beyond one, two or even three industries — a reflection of a deliberate effort by firms on both sides to learn from each other and forge partnerships across the globe," Stein said. According to a report released by the American Chamber of Commerce in South China earlier this year, 75 percent of enterprises it surveyed plan to reinvest in China in 2026, and over the next three to five years, its member companies are expected to reinvest $13.79 billion in profits generated in China. Gong Yu, founder and CEO of Chinese video-streaming company iQiyi — which Cook visited during his trip — said the ties between the two companies can be dated back to 2010. "Innovation in hardware, including the application of AI technology, has given us a particularly good synergy. This kind of mechanism allows us to achieve one plus one bigger than two, enabling this synergy to unleash even greater value," Gong said.
